proxy_language: Medieval and early modern Rhodian Greek (Dodecanesian Greek of the Hospitaller period and later), with Greek written in scholarly Latin transliteration; Hospitaller-era French/Italian court loans are a minor secondary layer
proxy_rationale: The culture label 'Roudòsach' (region Rodos, period index R, kind later_court) has no unambiguous attested language record; it most plausibly refers to the later court culture of Rhodes (Byzantine/Hospitaller/Ottoman-era island society). The best-supported proxy is the Greek of Rhodes and the Dodecanese, which is well documented in Medieval Greek texts (e.g., the Rhodian love poems, Hospitaller-period Greek documents) and in modern Dodecanesian dialect studies. The '-sach' ending in the label is not Greek morphology, and an Arabic/Turkish-style or Hospitaller-court reading cannot be excluded, so the link between the label and the proxy is weak. Names are built as Greek words in standard Romanization; no claim is made that 'Roudòsach' itself is attested.
phonology: Vowels: /a e i o u/ (5-vowel system; no phonemic length or diphthongs in Medieval/Modern Greek, spelled <ai ei oi ou> but pronounced as monophthongs). Consonants: stops /p t k b d g/ (in Dodecanesian often voiced stops from nasal+stop, mb nd ng); fricatives /f v θ ð s z x ɣ/; nasals /m n/; liquids /l r/; affricates /ts dz/ in many dialects. Dodecanesian traits: palatalization of /k/ before front vowels to /tʃ/ (kalos > tsalos-type shifts in Rhodian: 'tsi' for 'ki'), frequent voicing of stops after nasals, and mid-vowel raising in unstressed syllables (e>i, o>u). Stress is a dynamic accent on one of the last three syllables.
phonotactics: Syllables: (C)(C)V(C); onsets allow s+stop (st, sp, sk), stop+liquid (pr, tr, kr, pl, kl, gl, br, dr, gr), fricative+liquid (fr, vr, θr, xr, ɣl), and a few nasal clusters (mn, ks, ps, ts). Codas are mostly open or end in -s, -n, -r (word-final consonants limited to s, n, r, and occasionally l, k in loans); native words do not end in stops other than via loans. No word-initial ng, nk. Vowel hiatus is normally avoided or resolved by glide formation (i>j). Names end typically in vowels or -s/-n.
orthography: Scholarly Latin transliteration of Greek: a b g d e z i th k l m n x o p r s t y/i ph/f ch/kh ps; digraph vowels written as pronounced in Medieval/Modern romanization (ai>e, ei/oi/y>i, ou>u). Accents optional (stress marked with acute or grave on the stressed vowel). Use <th> for theta, <ch> for chi, <ph> for phi (or f in Modern Greek), <ng> for gamma+gamma/kappa, <mb nd> for mp/nt when voiced.
morphology: Highly inflected, suffixing. Nouns have three genders and (in the vernacular) four cases (nominative, genitive, accusative, vocative; dative lost). Common noun endings: masculine -os, -is, -as; feminine -a, -i, -is; neuter -o, -i, -ma. Plurals: -oi/-es/-a. Derivational suffixes: -tis/-tria (agent: 'maker'), -ia (abstract/place), -ikos/-iki (relational adjective), -ion/-aki (diminutive), -ma (result), -si(s) (action), -eio/-ion (place of), -on (neuter place). Adjectives agree in gender, number and case with the noun. Verbs: stem + person suffixes, aorist/imperfect augment; participles in -menos.
compounding: Compounds are head-final: first element (stem plus linking vowel -o-) modifies the second. E.g. thalassopoulos 'sea-bird', archi-tekton 'chief builder'. Agent compounds take verbal second elements: -ourgos, -poios, -phoros, -logos. 'X of Y' is expressed by genitive of Y after the noun (o naos tou iliou 'the temple of the sun') or by a compound. 'Y-maker' = Y-o-poios / Y-ourgos / Y-tis. Place names often take -ia, -ion, -eio. Linking vowel -o- is nearly universal, -i- or -a- occasionally.
noun_phrase_order: Article + adjective + noun (o megas naos) or article + noun + article + adjective (o naos o megas); genitive of possessor follows the head noun (o naos tou iliou); demonstratives precede (aftos o naos). Numerals and quantifiers precede the noun.

notes: Low confidence: the label Roudòsach and its '-sach' ending do not correspond to a clearly attested Greek word, so the proxy is Rhodian/Dodecanesian Medieval Greek by region and period, not by the culture name. The 'worked_examples' list is not populated here because patterns should be derived from the compounding and noun phrase rules above (e.g., 'Temple of the Sun' = naos tou iliou or iliou-naos; 'River Stew' = potamo-fagito; 'Harbour of the Rose' = limani tou rodou). No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word unless the language is Goidelic; this culture is Greek-based, so Gaelic forms must be avoided.
